newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs attack Croats at Christmas service - report.
newsitem.headline: Serbs attack Croats at Christmas service - report.

text.p: Serbs assaulted Croat refugees attending a Christmas Eve Catholic mass in the last enclave of Croatia under Serb control, injuring a U.N. worker, state media said on Wednesday.

The Croatian news agency HINA, quoting officials of the U.N. transitional administration in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), said 100 Serbs massed before the church in the town of Ilok, throwing explosive devices and insulting Croats.

HINA said some 50 Croat refugees, who had been bused into Eastern Slavonia to attend the mass, were trapped inside the church for three hours until UNTAES brought in military and civilian police reinforcements.
After the Croats left the church following the mass to have lunch in a nearby monastery, Serbs broke into the church, smashing windows and damaging the vestry, HINA said.
It said they also attacked several Croats and UNTAES personnel. HINA quoted UNTAES deputy spokesman Yuri Chizik as saying a U.N. policeman was injured in the disturbance.

UNTAES administrator Jacques Klein brought two senior Serb officials to the scene who persuaded the Serbs to disperse. But some stoned buses carrying Croats out of Ilok back to government-controlled territory to the west, HINA said.
Serbian media said the violence was provoked by Croat visitors who illegally brought in posters bearing Croatian insignia and shouted that Serbs were unwelcome in Croatia.
A semi-independent Serbian newspaper said UNTAES used tear gas and rifle butts against the Serb crowd.
UNTAES officials were unavailable for comment on Wednesday.

Armed minority Serbs seized almost a third of Croatia in a 1991 revolt against its move to independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia. But the Croatian army retook all rebel lands except Eastern Slavonia in two blitz offensives last year.

UNTAES, with 5,000 combat-trained peace troops, took charge of Eastern Slavonia last January with a mandate to gradually restore Croatian government rule in the region by mid-1997. The area's Serb militia was disbanded by UNTAES last summer.
Many thousands of the estimated 120,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia have applied for Croatian citizenship papers.

Others remain hostile to Croatian authority and some have demonstrated against the step-by-step reinstatement of Croatian institutions and an increasing number of UNTAES-assisted visits by Croat refugees preparing to resettle in their homes.
